title: Ravens, a Widow and a Living Son
sum: Without introduction, Elijah of Gilead stands before King Ahab and swears by the LORD that no dew or rain will fall until he says so. Then he disappears. God hides him by a brook east of the Jordan, where ravens bring him food, and when the brook dries up God sends him north into Phoenicia, Jezebel's own country, to a widow gathering sticks for her last meal. Her flour and oil never run out.

When the widow's son dies, she blames the prophet. Elijah carries the boy upstairs, cries out to God, stretches himself over him three times, and the boy breathes again. The chapter that began with Elijah's word ends with a foreign woman's confession: "the LORD's word in your mouth is true." Every scene asks the same question the drought asks: who really gives rain, bread and life, Baal or the LORD?
readings: Read as history

Traditional Jewish and Christian readers take the chapter as a record of real events in Ahab's reign, about 860 BC. A Phoenician history quoted by Josephus remembers a drought in the reign of Jezebel's father, and Zarephath is a real town that has been excavated. The miracles are God's acts in history, like those of the exodus.
Read as prophetic legend

Many critical scholars see stories told and retold among the prophets' disciples, like the Elisha stories of 2 Kings 4, which have close parallels: a widow's oil, a dead son, a prophet stretched on a child. On this view the stories teach what kind of man Elijah was and what kind of God he served, whatever happened in detail.
Read as theology against Baal

Literary readers notice that every scene answers a claim of Baal worship: Baal brings rain, Baal gives grain and oil, Baal returns from Death. Here the LORD shuts the sky, feeds a widow in Baal's own land and raises a dead boy. The chapter is a quiet contest before the loud one on Carmel.

views.H: The drought is real and long; the ravens, the jar and the raising are miracles, signs that the God of Israel rules even in Phoenicia. Elijah's oath shows a prophet acting on God's word (James 5:17 reads it as prayer).
views.C: Critical scholars usually treat chapters 17–19 as an Elijah cycle that a Deuteronomistic editor fitted into the reign of Ahab. Chapter 17 may join three originally separate stories, held together by the drought frame and the theme of the word of the LORD (17:2, 17:8, 17:16, 17:24).
views.A: Excavations at Sarafand (Zarephath) show a Phoenician town of potters and traders with a shrine to Tanit-Astarte. Josephus, quoting Menander of Ephesus, reports a year-long drought under Ithobaal of Tyre. The Ugaritic myths show what Baal was believed to do: bring dew and rain, and return from Death.
views.J: The Talmud says the keys of rain, birth and the raising of the dead belong to God alone, and that Elijah had to hand back the key of rain to receive the key of the dead (Bavli Sanhedrin 113a); tradition also made the widow's son the prophet Jonah.
views.X: Jesus used the widow of Zarephath to show that God's mercy reached a foreigner when Israel would not receive its prophet (Luke 4:25–26), and Luke tells the raising at Nain in words that echo 17:23 (Luke 7:15). Hebrews counts this among the women who took back their dead through resurrection (Hebrews 11:35).

deep.b: Readers have long noticed how closely the stories of Elijah and Elisha mirror each other. Both help a widow with a supply of oil (17:14–16; 2 Kings 4:1–7). Both lodge in an upper room and raise a dead boy by lying on him (17:19–22; 2 Kings 4:32–37). Both call down judgment and both part the Jordan with the same cloak (2 Kings 2:8, 2:14). Some scholars think stories about one prophet were transferred to the other; others think the narrator shaped them in pairs on purpose, to show that Elisha truly received a double share of Elijah's spirit (2 Kings 2:9–15). The gospels draw on both, especially in the raising at Nain and the feeding stories.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a drought aimed at Baal's three gifts
deep.b: This is my own reading, though it builds on the common observation that chapters 17–18 are a polemic against Baal. The Ugaritic Baal was said to give three things: rain and dew, the fruit of the earth (grain, wine and oil), and life restored after Death. I suggest that chapter 17 is arranged to take each away from him in turn. 17:1 claims the dew and rain for the LORD. 17:8–16 has the LORD give flour and oil in Baal's own land, while the land lies dry. 17:17–24 has the LORD, not Baal, bring a boy back from death. Carmel then settles in public what Zarephath showed in private. If the reading is right, the widow's confession in 17:24 is the chapter's answer to the question Elijah will put to all Israel in 18:21.

echoes: Deuteronomy 11:16–17; Deuteronomy 28:23–24; 2 Kings 4:1–37; Luke 4:25–26; Luke 7:11–17; James 5:17; Hebrews 11:35; Revelation 11:6

settings.when: after Ahab has married Jezebel and built a temple for Baal in Samaria
settings.why: Elijah swears by the life of the LORD, whom he serves, that there will be no dew or rain except at his word. Baal was worshiped as the god of storm and rain. The drought is a direct challenge: the LORD, not Baal, controls the rain. Readers who knew Deuteronomy's warning that rain would stop if Israel served other gods (Deuteronomy 11:16–17) saw it carried out.

settings.what: The LORD sends Elijah to the Kerith Brook
settings.when: just after he announces the drought to Ahab
settings.why: God tells Elijah to hide east of the Jordan, and says ravens will feed him there. The prophet who stopped the rain is kept alive by God in the drought. Readers see that the LORD, not the king, controls who lives through it.

settings.what: The LORD sends Elijah to Zarephath
settings.when: when the Kerith Brook dries up
settings.why: God sends Elijah to Zarephath, a town of Sidon, where he has ordered a widow to feed him. Sidon was Jezebel's home and a center of Baal worship. God shows his power in Baal's own land, and through the poorest of its people.

settings.what: Elijah's promise to the widow of Zarephath
settings.by: Elijah, speaking for the LORD, the God of Israel
settings.to: a widow gathering sticks at the gate of Zarephath, a town of Sidon
settings.when: when she has only a handful of flour and a little oil left before she and her son die
settings.why: Elijah tells her not to fear, to make him a small loaf first, and promises that her flour and oil will not run out until the rain comes. The promise is made to a foreign widow in Jezebel's own homeland, the heart of Baal country. The LORD feeds her where Baal cannot. Jesus pointed to her to show that God's mercy reached outsiders (Luke 4:25–26).

settings.what: Elijah's prayer for the widow's son
settings.to: the LORD his God, in the upstairs room
settings.when: after the widow's son stops breathing and she blames the prophet
settings.why: Elijah asks God why he has brought harm on the widow who gave him shelter, and three times stretches out on the boy, praying for his life to return. The prayer is bold, even accusing. The boy lives. It shows readers that the LORD has power over death, the realm the Canaanites gave to the god Mot.

settings.when: when he brings her son down alive
settings.why: She says, "you are a man of God, and the LORD's word in your mouth is true." A foreign woman reaches the confession that Israel will reach only on Carmel (18:39). The book's theme, that the LORD's word is true, is spoken by an outsider.

title: Fire on Carmel
sum: In the third year of the drought, God sends Elijah back to Ahab. On the way he meets Obadiah, Ahab's steward, who has secretly hidden a hundred of the LORD's prophets from Jezebel. Ahab greets Elijah as "the one who brings trouble on Israel"; Elijah answers that the king is the trouble. He calls for all Israel and the 450 prophets of Baal to meet him on Mount Carmel.

There Elijah asks the people how long they will limp along on two crutches, and sets a test: each side will prepare a bull, and the god who answers with fire is God. Baal's prophets cry out, dance and gash themselves from morning until afternoon, and there is not a sound. Elijah rebuilds the LORD's altar with twelve stones, drenches it with water, and prays a short prayer. Fire falls. The people cry, "The LORD, he is the God!" The prophets of Baal are killed at the Kishon River, and Elijah crouches on the mountain until a cloud like a hand rises from the sea and the rain comes.
readings: Read as history

Many Jewish and Christian readers take the contest as a real public event, a turning point when the LORD proved himself before Israel. The altar, the time of the afternoon offering, the place on Carmel and the Kishon fit the geography and the worship of the time.
Read as legend or composite story

Critical scholars often see two stories joined: a drought story (18:1–18, 18:41–46) and a contest story (18:19–40). The numbers and the scale may have grown in the telling, and the slaughter may reflect later struggles against Baal worship, perhaps in Jehu's or Josiah's time (2 Kings 10; 2 Kings 23).
Read as theology

However it happened, the story makes one claim in many ways: the LORD does what Baal was believed to do, sends fire and rain, and Israel cannot serve both. The questions of 18:21 and 18:24 are put to every reader.

views.H: A real contest at a real place, probably near el-Muhraqa on the southeast of the Carmel ridge. Elijah acted under the law of Deuteronomy 13 and 17 in killing the prophets who led Israel to Baal. The rain followed as God had promised in 18:1.
views.C: The chapter shows Deuteronomistic concerns (the twelve tribes, the one God, the false prophets) laid over older Elijah traditions. Many scholars think its picture of a nation-wide turning to the LORD is idealized, since Baal worship continues in 2 Kings 1 and 10. The 400 prophets of Asherah are often taken as an addition.
views.A: Ugaritic texts describe Baal as the cloud-rider who flashes lightning and sends rain, and show the god El gashing himself in mourning, as Baal's prophets do here. Tacitus knew of an altar and a god on Carmel with no image. The Egyptian story of Wenamun describes ecstatic prophecy at Byblos, on the Phoenician coast.
views.J: 18:1–39 is read in synagogues alongside the golden calf story (Exodus 32), and the people's cry "The LORD, he is the God" is said seven times at the close of Yom Kippur. The Talmud explains the altar outside Jerusalem as a prophet's emergency ruling (Bavli Yevamot 90b) and says Elijah was answered at the hour of the afternoon prayer (Bavli Berakhot 6b).
views.X: James holds up Elijah's prayer for rain (James 5:17–18). Jesus refuses to call down fire like Elijah (Luke 9:54–55), and Revelation warns that a false prophet can also bring fire from the sky (Revelation 13:13). Christian readers have seen in the twelve stones the one people of God and in the fire God's acceptance of a sacrifice.

deep.h: The slaughter at the Kishon: how readers have judged it
deep.b: Verse 40 is short and brutal: the prophets of Baal are seized and killed. Readers have taken four main positions. Covenant justice: Deuteronomy commands death for a prophet who leads Israel to other gods (Deuteronomy 13:1–5), and Jezebel had already killed the LORD's prophets (18:4, 18:13); Elijah acts as Moses' Levites did after the golden calf (Exodus 32:26–28). Justified then, not now: many Jewish and Christian teachers accept the act in its setting but deny it is a model, pointing to Jesus' rebuke of the disciples who wanted fire (Luke 9:54–55). Critique within the tradition: the rabbis say Elijah upheld God's honor but not Israel's (Mekhilta, Pisha 1), and some readers see chapter 19, where God is not in the fire, as a quiet correction. Readers also notice that no command from God for the killing is recorded: Elijah gives the order himself, though at the altar he had said he acted "because you told me to" (18:36). Critical history: some scholars think the slaughter belongs to later polemic and was never a historical event on this scale. This site presents the text as it stands and these readings side by side.

deep.h: A note on the numbers and the water
deep.b: Readers ask where twelve jars of water came from after three years of drought. The Mediterranean lies below Carmel, and springs on the mountain may have kept flowing. Josephus says the water came from a spring. The 450 prophets, the twelve stones and the repeated pouring are part of a carefully shaped story in which everything is counted and nothing is hidden.

echoes: Deuteronomy 13:1–5; Deuteronomy 4:35; Exodus 32:26–28; Joshua 24:15; Leviticus 9:24; Judges 6:25–32; Luke 9:54–55; James 5:17–18; Revelation 13:13; Malachi 4:5–6

settings.when: in the third year of the drought
settings.why: God tells Elijah to show himself to Ahab, because he is about to send rain. The word sets up the contest on Carmel. The rain will come from the LORD, the God Elijah serves, not from Baal.

settings.by: Obadiah, manager of Ahab's palace and a man who feared the LORD
settings.when: in the third year of drought, when Elijah tells him to announce his return to Ahab
settings.why: Obadiah protests that Ahab has searched every nation for Elijah, and that if the Spirit carries Elijah off, Ahab will kill him. He reminds Elijah that he hid a hundred of the LORD's prophets from Jezebel. The speech shows readers that faithful people still served inside Ahab's court, at great risk. Elijah is not as alone as he thinks (compare 19:18).

settings.when: at the end of the drought
settings.why: Ahab calls Elijah the one who brings trouble on Israel. Elijah throws the charge back: Ahab and his father's house brought it by leaving the LORD's commands for the Baals. Then he calls for all Israel and the prophets of Baal and Asherah to gather on Mount Carmel. The exchange sets the question the contest will answer: whose fault is the drought, and who is God?

settings.to: all the people of Israel gathered on Mount Carmel, with the 450 prophets of Baal
settings.when: before the contest
settings.why: Elijah asks how long they will limp between two opinions: if the LORD is God, follow him; if Baal, follow Baal. He proposes a test: the god who answers by fire is God. The people agree. The challenge is aimed at Israelites who tried to worship both. For later readers in exile among other gods, it put the same choice before them.

settings.what: Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal
settings.to: the prophets of Baal, dancing and crying out around their altar
settings.when: at noon, when Baal has not answered
settings.why: Elijah tells them to shout louder, since Baal is a god: he may be thinking, or stepped away, or traveling, or asleep. The mockery plays on the stories of Baal told in Canaanite myth, in which Baal could be absent, and even die and come back to life. It is meant to show the people how empty Baal worship is. Gary Rendsburg argued that two of the words ("lost in thought" and "stepped away") are polite ways of saying Baal had gone to relieve himself. That reading is found already in the Targum and Rashi.

settings.to: the LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, beside the soaked altar of twelve stones
settings.when: at the hour of the evening grain offering
settings.why: Elijah's short prayer asks God to show that he is God in Israel, that Elijah is his servant, and that God is turning the people's hearts back. The calm prayer stands against hours of shouting. Fire falls. The twelve stones and the name of Jacob called "Israel" remind the northern tribes that they are still one people of the LORD.

settings.by: all the people of Israel on Mount Carmel
settings.to: the LORD, falling on their faces
settings.when: when fire consumes the offering, the stones and the water
settings.why: They cry, "The LORD, he is the God!" In Hebrew the words echo Elijah's own name, which means "my God is the LORD." The confession is what the whole contest was for. It answers Elijah's question in 18:21.

settings.when: after the fire falls on Carmel and the prophets of Baal are killed
settings.why: Elijah tells Ahab to eat and drink, because he hears the roar of rain. Then he prays on the mountaintop and sends his servant seven times to look at the sea, until a cloud as small as a hand appears. The drought that began with Elijah's word ends with his word and his prayer. James 5:17–18 holds this up as a model of prayer.

traditions.q: Elijah had the prophets of Baal killed (1 Kings 18:40). May rulers punish false religion?
views: For centuries Church law said yes: the Fourth Lateran Council (1215) told rulers to drive heretics out of their lands. The Second Vatican Council taught instead that no one may be forced to act against conscience in religion, within the just limits of public order (Dignitatis Humanae 2).

Luther first wrote that heresy is a spiritual matter that cannot be fought with fire (Temporal Authority, 1523). Later he and Melanchthon backed punishing Anabaptists, mainly as rebels and blasphemers. Lutheran churches today teach religious freedom.

Calvin defended the execution of Servetus (1553) from the Old Testament laws against false prophets. The Westminster Confession gave rulers a duty to suppress heresy (23.3), but American Presbyterians rewrote the article in 1788, so that the state has no power over faith.

No. The sword is ordained outside the perfection of Christ, and in the church the only penalty is to be put out (Schleitheim Confession 6, 1527). Balthasar Hubmaier wrote in 1524 that those who burn heretics are the worst heretics of all, and many Anabaptists died at the hands of rulers.

No. Thomas Helwys (1612) and Roger Williams (1644) argued that Israel under the Law was a nation without equal, a picture of the church, and no pattern for any state, so rulers must leave conscience free. The Baptist Faith and Message teaches full religious liberty (article 17).

title: The Sound of Thin Silence
sum: After Carmel, Jezebel swears to kill Elijah by the next day, and the prophet runs. He leaves his servant at Beersheba, walks a day into the wilderness, sits under a broom bush and asks to die. An angel wakes him twice with bread and water, and on the strength of that food he walks forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God, where Moses received the covenant.

There God asks, "Why are you here, Elijah?" Elijah says he alone is left. A wind tears the mountains, a quake shakes them, fire passes, but the LORD is not in any of them; then comes "a sound of thin silence." Elijah covers his face and hears the same question, and gives the same answer. God sends him back with three tasks, to anoint Hazael, Jehu and Elisha, and tells him that seven thousand in Israel have not bowed to Baal. Elijah throws his cloak over Elisha, who leaves his oxen and follows him.
readings: Read as a prophet's crisis

Many readers see a portrait of burnout and depression after a great victory: fear, flight, a wish to die. God answers with sleep, food, a journey, a question, and a new task. The story has comforted many in despair.
Read as a new Moses

The chapter retraces Moses' story: forty days, the mountain of God, a cave like the cleft of the rock, a covered face, God passing by, and a successor (Elisha as Joshua). Elijah is the prophet who goes back to the source of the covenant to see whether it still holds.
Read as a correction of Carmel

Some readers see God gently correcting Elijah: the LORD who answered with fire on Carmel is not in the fire at Horeb, and Elijah's sense of being the only faithful one is wrong. Others think this reads too much into the scene: God does not rebuke Elijah, and the three anointings continue his work.

views.H: A real journey to Sinai in the 850s BC, and a real encounter with God. The three anointings are fulfilled by Elijah and his successor: Elisha at once, Hazael and Jehu by Elisha's word (2 Kings 8–9).
views.C: Many critical scholars think chapter 19 was shaped, perhaps during the exile, as a deliberate parallel to Exodus 33–34, a meditation on how God is present when the old signs fail. The anointing commands may be added to tie Elijah to later events in 2 Kings.
views.A: Hazael is named in Assyrian records as the usurper "son of a nobody" who seized Damascus about 842 BC; Jehu appears on the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III bowing to the Assyrian king. The broom bush is the white broom of the Negev. The location of Horeb is still debated.
views.J: Jewish tradition says the cave was the same one where Moses stood (Bavli Pesahim 54a), identifies Elijah's zeal with that of Phinehas (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 47), and turns his complaint that Israel abandoned the covenant into the custom of Elijah's chair at every circumcision (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 29). 18:46–19:21 is read in synagogues with the Torah portion on Phinehas.
views.X: Paul uses the seven thousand to speak of a remnant chosen by grace (Romans 11:2–5). Jesus' forty days in the wilderness recall Moses' and Elijah's (Matthew 4:2), and on the mountain of the Transfiguration Elijah, with Moses, finally sees God's glory in Jesus (Mark 9:2–8). The call of Elisha lies behind Jesus' sayings about following him (Luke 9:61–62).

deep.h: Qol demamah daqqah: the readings and the choice
deep.b:
The three words of 19:12 have been translated in at least five ways. The Greek translation says "a sound of a light breeze" and the Latin "the whistling of a gentle breeze": after the storm, a soft wind. The Aramaic Targum makes it the sound of angels praising God in silence. The KJV, through earlier English Bibles, made "a still small voice" famous, and generations heard in it God's quiet inward voice. Many modern versions say "a gentle whisper" or "a low whisper." Literal renderings, "a sound of thin silence" or "the sound of sheer silence," keep the paradox of a sound that is silence, and a few scholars have even argued for a thunderous roar.

This translation chooses "a sound of thin silence" for three reasons. First, demamah elsewhere means silence or calm (Psalm 107:29; Job 4:16), and daqqah means thin or fine (Exodus 16:14). Second, the voice that speaks comes only in the next verse (19:13); "voice" or "whisper" in 19:12 adds speech the text has not yet given. Third, the paradox seems intended: after wind, quake and fire, the LORD comes in what is almost nothing. Readers who prefer "whisper" or "breeze" have good arguments too, and the note on 19:12 sets them out.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Elijah's unchanged answer is the point
deep.b: This is my own reading, though several literary critics (for example Jerome Walsh) make similar observations. God asks Elijah the same question twice, before and after the theophany (19:9, 19:13), and Elijah gives the same answer word for word (19:10, 19:14). I suggest the narrator repeats the answer exactly so that the reader notices what did not change. The vision of the thin silence was meant to move Elijah from the logic of fire to the logic of patience, and he does not move. So God's reply both honors and replaces him: it gives him three tasks whose fulfillment lies years ahead, beyond his own lifetime for two of them, and it names his successor. The seven thousand answer "I alone am left." On this reading, Horeb is not a rebuke but a retirement, gently given.

echoes: Exodus 3:1–6; Exodus 24:18; Exodus 33:18–23; Exodus 34:5–6; Exodus 34:28; Numbers 11:15; Jonah 4:3; Numbers 25:11; Romans 11:2–5; Luke 9:61–62; Matthew 4:2; Mark 9:2–8; Hebrews 11:37

settings.when: after Ahab tells her Elijah has killed the prophets of Baal
settings.why: Jezebel swears by her gods that by this time tomorrow Elijah will be dead like her prophets. The day after the victory on Carmel, one message sends Elijah running. Readers see that one great sign does not end the struggle, and that the prophet is a man like them (James 5:17).

settings.to: the LORD, under a broom bush in the wilderness south of Beersheba
settings.when: after a day's walk into the wilderness, fleeing Jezebel
settings.why: Elijah says he has had enough and asks God to take his life, since he is no better than his fathers. God answers with food and sleep, not a rebuke. The prayer shows readers that despair can come to the faithful, and that God cares for the whole person.

settings.what: The LORD meets Elijah at Horeb
settings.to: Elijah, in the cave at Horeb, the mountain of God; and the LORD
settings.when: after forty days and nights of walking
settings.why: God asks twice, "Why are you here, Elijah?" Elijah complains that Israel has broken the covenant, killed the prophets, and that he alone is left. Between the two answers God passes by, not in wind, earthquake or fire, but in "a sound of thin silence." At the mountain where Moses received the covenant (Exodus 33:18–23), Elijah learns that God is not only in the dramatic signs of Carmel.
views: Many readers take the silence as a lesson that God speaks gently and quietly.
Others note that Elijah gives the same answer before and after. They read the scene as God gently correcting his belief that he is alone and that only force will work.
Most take the Hebrew qol demamah daqqah as "a sound of thin silence" or a whisper. Johan Lust argued it may instead mean a roaring, thundering sound, like the thunder at Sinai.

settings.what: The LORD's commission: three to anoint
settings.when: after Elijah's second complaint
settings.why: God sends Elijah back to anoint Hazael king of Aram, Jehu king of Israel, and Elisha as prophet in his place. He tells him seven thousand in Israel have not bowed to Baal. Elijah is not alone, and his work is not finished. The commission points ahead to 2 Kings, where Elisha carries it out. Paul used the seven thousand to speak of a faithful remnant (Romans 11:2–5).

settings.to: Elisha son of Shaphat, plowing with twelve pairs of oxen; then Elijah
settings.when: after Elijah leaves Horeb
settings.why: Elijah throws his cloak on Elisha, which marks him as Elijah's successor. Elisha asks to kiss his parents goodbye. Elijah's answer, "What have I done to you?", leaves the choice to him. Elisha sacrifices his oxen, feeds the people and follows. It is the first step in carrying out God's command at Horeb (19:16). Jesus' words about putting a hand to the plow (Luke 9:61–62) echo it.

title: The God of Hills and Valleys
sum: Ben-hadad of Damascus, with thirty-two allied kings, surrounds Samaria and demands Ahab's silver, gold, wives and children. Ahab gives in to the first demand but refuses the second, and answers Ben-hadad's boast with a proverb: the man putting on his armor should not brag like the man taking it off. A prophet promises victory through a small band of young officers, and while Ben-hadad drinks in his shelters, Israel routs his army.

The Arameans decide that Israel's god is a god of the mountains and fight the next year on the plain at Aphek. A man of God promises that the LORD will show himself God of the valleys too, and Aram is crushed. But when Ben-hadad's servants come in sackcloth begging for his life, Ahab calls him "my brother," makes a treaty and lets him go. A prophet, disguised as a wounded soldier, tricks Ahab into pronouncing his own sentence: because he let go the man the LORD had put under the ban, his life will go for Ben-hadad's life.
readings: Read as history

Traditional readers take the two campaigns as real wars of the 850s BC. The treaty of 20:34 fits the Assyrian record that at Qarqar in 853 BC Ahab and the king of Damascus fought together, and the chapter explains how they came to be allies.
Read as a story from another reign

Following J. Maxwell Miller, many historians think the wars of chapters 20 and 22 first belonged to the later Jehu dynasty, when Israel really was weak before Damascus (2 Kings 13), and that an editor later named the unnamed "king of Israel" as Ahab. The Assyrian evidence of an Ahab–Damascus alliance, and the name Hadadezer for the king of Damascus in 853 BC, are their main arguments.
Read as a lesson about God's name

The chapter's refrain is "you will know that I am the LORD" (20:13, 20:28). God helps even Ahab, not as a reward but to prove that he rules hills and valleys alike. The last scene shows what happens when the king treats God's victory as his own to bargain with.

views.H: Real battles, real prophets, and a king who won by God's help and then threw away God's victory for a political deal. The prophet's acted parable condemns him as Nathan condemned David.
views.C: A different source from the Elijah stories: prophets here are court advisers in war, the king is often unnamed, and Ahab is portrayed more favorably. The final scene (20:35–43) brings the story into line with the Deuteronomistic judgment on Ahab.
views.A: Ben-hadad ("son of Hadad") was a throne name in Damascus; Assyrian texts name Hadadezer as king of Damascus in 853 BC and record his alliance with Ahab at Qarqar. Trade quarters abroad, like the "streets" of 20:34, are well known from the ancient Near East.
views.J: Rabbinic readers debated Ahab's mercy: was it kindness or rebellion against God's word? Many compare Saul's sparing of Agag (1 Samuel 15). The phrase "kings of loyal love" (20:31) was taken as a compliment to Israel's kings even from their enemies.
views.X: Christian readers have often used the chapter to show that God's grace to the undeserving does not cancel his judgment, and that the parable (20:39–40) works as Nathan's did and as Jesus' parables do, drawing the hearer into judging himself (Matthew 21:33–41).

deep.h: Ahab, Ben-hadad and the Kurkh Monolith
deep.b:
The chapter 16 page describes the Kurkh Monolith and the battle of Qarqar. In brief: in 853 BC Shalmaneser III of Assyria fought a coalition at Qarqar on the Orontes. His Kurkh Monolith lists the allies: Hadadezer of Damascus with 1,200 chariots, 1,200 horsemen and 20,000 soldiers; Irhuleni of Hamath; and "Ahab the Israelite" with 2,000 chariots and 10,000 soldiers, among others. Shalmaneser claims a great victory, but he had to return several times in the following years, so the alliance held for a while.

How does this fit 1 Kings 20 and 22? Three main answers have been offered. (1) The wars of chapter 20 came before Qarqar, and the treaty of 20:34 made the alliance possible; after the Assyrian threat passed, the old quarrel over Ramoth-gilead broke out again (22:1–3). (2) "Ben-hadad" was a title or second name of Hadadezer. (3) The stories first belonged to a later period and were attached to Ahab. The Bible itself never mentions Qarqar, which shows that the writer of Kings chose what to tell for reasons other than political history.

echoes: 1 Samuel 15:8–23; 2 Samuel 12:1–7; Deuteronomy 7:2; Deuteronomy 20:16–17; 13:24; 2 Kings 13:14–25; Amos 1:3–5

settings.by: Ben-hadad king of Aram, then Ahab king of Israel and the elders
settings.to: Ahab, besieged in Samaria; then Ben-hadad, through messengers
settings.when: when Ben-hadad and thirty-two allied kings surround Samaria
settings.why: Ben-hadad first claims Ahab's silver, gold, wives and children, and Ahab gives in. When Ben-hadad demands the right to search and take whatever he likes, Ahab, backed by the elders, refuses. He sends a proverb: the man putting on his armor should not boast like the man taking it off. The exchange shows a weak king finding courage, and sets up a victory God will give.

settings.by: an unnamed prophet, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Ahab king of Israel, in Samaria
settings.when: as the Aramean army takes up position
settings.why: God promises to hand the huge army to Ahab, through the young men of the district officials, "Then you will know that I am the LORD." The LORD fights for Israel even under Ahab, the worst of its kings. The aim is that the king will come to know him.

settings.when: after the victory at Samaria
settings.why: The prophet warns Ahab to strengthen himself, because the king of Aram will return in the spring. God's help includes good advice, and it calls the king to prepare.

settings.what: The Arameans' theory of Israel's god
settings.by: the servants of the king of Aram
settings.when: after their defeat
settings.why: They say Israel's god is a god of the mountains, so they should fight on the plain, and replace the kings with governors. Like many ancient people, they think each god rules one territory. The speech sets up God's answer through the man of God (20:28).

settings.what: The man of God's word before Aphek
settings.by: a man of God, speaking for the LORD
settings.when: as the small Israelite army faces Aram's huge army at Aphek
settings.why: Because Aram has said the LORD is a god of mountains and not of valleys, God will hand the army over, "Then you will know that I am the LORD." The battle becomes a test of whether Israel's God rules everywhere. Readers in exile, far from Israel's hills, needed to know he did.

settings.by: Ben-hadad's servants, then Ahab and Ben-hadad
settings.when: after Aram's defeat at Aphek, when Ben-hadad is hiding in the city
settings.why: Ben-hadad's servants come in sackcloth, saying Israel's kings are known for loyal love. Ahab calls Ben-hadad "my brother," and they make a covenant: Ben-hadad returns towns and gives Israel trading rights in Damascus. The treaty is good politics, but Ahab has let go a king the LORD handed over to him. The next scene judges it.

settings.what: A prophet's trap for the king
settings.by: one of the sons of the prophets, disguised as a wounded soldier
settings.to: Ahab king of Israel, as he passes by the road
settings.when: after Ahab releases Ben-hadad
settings.why: Like Nathan's parable, this is a trap. The prophet gets himself wounded and bandaged, then tells the king a made-up case: he was guarding a prisoner who escaped, and owes his life or a talent of silver. Ahab gives his verdict at once: "You have settled it yourself." Then the prophet takes off the bandage and turns the verdict on Ahab. Because Ahab let go the man God had put under the ban, his life will go for that man's life, "and your people for his people." The judgment reaches Israel too. The king who judged the soldier has judged himself. Readers see that God's word cannot be escaped by a king's clever treaty.
views: Uriel Simon grouped this with Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:1–4) and the wise woman of Tekoa (2 Samuel 14:4–20). Each is a legal case told to lead the hearer to judge himself.

Many readers find the death of the prophet who would not strike his friend hard to accept. The story makes the point that God's command must be obeyed even when it seems strange, which is the very failure of Ahab.

title: Naboth's Vineyard
sum: Ahab wants the vineyard next to his palace in Jezreel and offers Naboth a better one or a fair price. Naboth refuses: the LORD forbid that he give away his fathers' inheritance. Ahab goes home and sulks. Jezebel takes over. In letters sealed with the king's seal she orders the elders of Naboth's town to call a fast, seat Naboth in front, and bring in two worthless men to swear that he cursed God and the king. They do, and Naboth is stoned. Ahab goes down to take the vineyard.

Elijah meets him there with God's question: "Have you murdered, and taken possession as well?" The dogs that licked Naboth's blood will lick Ahab's; his house will be wiped out like those of Jeroboam and Baasha; dogs will eat Jezebel by the rampart of Jezreel. Then the worst king of Israel tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and fasts, and the LORD tells Elijah that, because Ahab has humbled himself, the disaster will come in his son's days instead.
readings: Read as a story about justice

The chapter is the Bible's classic case of a ruler abusing law and religion to take a poor man's land. Naboth stands on the covenant: the land belongs to the LORD. The prophet holds the king to the same law as everyone else. Readers in every age have seen their own rulers in it.
Read as a study in two characters

Literary readers watch Ahab and Jezebel: the king who wants but will not act, and the queen who acts without scruple. Some read Jezebel as the narrator's villain, others as a woman whose portrait was drawn by her enemies. Both readings agree that Ahab cannot hide behind her: Elijah charges him with the murder.
Read as a story of repentance

The ending surprises: the LORD notices Ahab's humility and delays the judgment. Jewish and Christian teachers have used it to show that no one is beyond the reach of repentance, and also to ask why the punishment falls on Ahab's son.

views.H: A real crime in Jezreel, about 855 BC, and a real prophetic sentence that came true in 22:38 and in Jehu's coup (2 Kings 9:21–37). The narrator holds Ahab responsible for what his wife did in his name.
views.C: Many critical scholars think the story was expanded: an original prophecy against Ahab (21:17–20) was enlarged with Deuteronomistic language (21:20b–26) and a note on Ahab's repentance (21:27–29) that explains why he died in battle rather than at Jezreel. The differences between 21:19, 22:38 and 2 Kings 9:25–26 suggest more than one tradition about the end of Ahab's house.
views.A: Excavations at Jezreel have uncovered a large ninth-century royal enclosure, and the region is full of ancient wine presses. Seals were used to authorize letters, and a seal inscribed with the name Jezebel is known, though whether it was the queen's is debated. The Greek puts this chapter before chapter 20 (see the variant at 21:1).
views.J: The Talmud asks whether property of a man executed by the king goes to the crown, using Naboth as its example (Bavli Sanhedrin 48b), and later identifies the spirit of 22:21 as Naboth's, seeking justice. Rabbinic tradition also takes Ahab's repentance seriously as genuine.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Naboth, condemned by false witnesses for blasphemy and taken outside the city to die, a picture of Jesus (Mark 14:55–64; Hebrews 13:12) and of Stephen (Acts 6:11–13; Acts 7:58). The passage has also been central in Christian teaching on social justice and on the limits of state power.

deep.b: Naboth's answer is not stubbornness but faith. Israel's law held that the land belonged to the LORD, who gave each family its share: "The land must not be sold for good, because the land is mine" (Leviticus 25:23). Land could be leased until the year of Jubilee, but not sold away from the family (Leviticus 25:13–28), and inheritances were not to move from tribe to tribe (Numbers 36:7). Samuel had warned that a king would take the people's fields and vineyards (1 Samuel 8:14), and Ezekiel later forbids the prince to seize the people's inheritance (Ezekiel 46:18). Jezebel, whom the story presents as caring nothing for such laws, uses the forms of Israel's own law, a fast, two witnesses, a charge of blasphemy, to destroy a man who kept it.

deep.title: Claude's theory: two councils, two lies
deep.b: This is my own reading, though it overlaps with the rabbinic idea that the lying spirit of 22:21 was the spirit of Naboth (Bavli Sanhedrin 89a). In the Hebrew order chapter 21 is followed directly by chapter 22, and the two chapters mirror each other. In chapter 21 an earthly court, the elders of Jezreel, receives sealed letters from the palace, sends two worthless men to speak a lie, and brings an innocent man to his death. In chapter 22 the heavenly court, the LORD's council, sends a spirit to speak a lie through four hundred prophets, and brings the guilty king to his death. The measure Ahab's house used is measured back to it: a court, a lie and a death. If this is right, it is one argument for the Hebrew order of chapters 20–22 over the Greek, which separates the two scenes (see the variant at 21:1).

echoes: Leviticus 25:23; Numbers 36:7; 1 Samuel 8:14; Deuteronomy 17:6; Exodus 20:13–17; Exodus 22:28; 2 Samuel 12:1–14; 2 Kings 9:21–37; Micah 2:1–2; Isaiah 5:8; Acts 6:11–13

settings.by: King Ahab, then Naboth of Jezreel
settings.when: when Ahab wants Naboth's vineyard next to the palace in Jezreel for a vegetable garden
settings.why: Ahab makes a fair offer of a better vineyard or money. Naboth refuses with an oath: "The LORD keep me from giving you my fathers' inheritance!" The law taught that the land belongs to the LORD and that each family's share must stay in the family (Leviticus 25:23; Numbers 36:7). Naboth's refusal is faithfulness to that law, which bound king and farmer alike. Ahab seems to know it, which is why he sulks rather than acts.

settings.when: after Naboth's refusal
settings.why: Jezebel asks, "Is that any way for you to rule as king over Israel?" and promises to get the vineyard herself. She speaks from a view of kingship, common among the kings of Phoenicia, in which the king can take what he wants. Israel's law held the king under God's law. Her words show readers what Samuel had warned a king would do (1 Samuel 8:14).

settings.by: Jezebel, writing in Ahab's name and sealed with his seal
settings.to: the elders and leading men of Jezreel, Naboth's town
settings.when: right after her promise to Ahab
settings.why: The letters order a fast, two worthless men to accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king, and his stoning. The plot turns Israel's own law against an innocent man: the law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6) and punished cursing God by stoning (Leviticus 24:16). The town's leaders obey. Readers see how a ruler can use the forms of justice to murder, and how the whole town shares the guilt.

settings.what: Elijah's word to Ahab in the vineyard
settings.when: as Ahab goes down to take possession
settings.why: God's question is sharp: "Have you murdered, and taken possession as well?" The sentence fits the crime: where dogs licked Naboth's blood, they will lick Ahab's. Ahab's house will be cut off like Jeroboam's and Baasha's, and dogs will eat Jezebel at Jezreel. The word makes clear to readers that the LORD defends the poor man's land against the king. It comes true in part at Ahab's death (22:38). Because Ahab humbles himself, the rest is put off to his son (21:29), and it is fulfilled for Joram and Jezebel in 2 Kings 9:25–37.

settings.what: The LORD's word about Ahab's repentance
settings.when: after Ahab tears his clothes, wears sackcloth and fasts
settings.why: God points out to Elijah that Ahab has humbled himself, and delays the disaster to his son's days. Even the worst king can find mercy when he humbles himself. For readers in exile, that was hope: repentance still matters to God, though it may not undo all the consequences.

title: Micaiah and the Lying Spirit
sum: After three years of peace, Ahab asks Jehoshaphat of Judah to help him take back Ramoth-gilead from Aram. Jehoshaphat agrees but asks for a word from the LORD. Four hundred prophets say, "Go up." Jehoshaphat asks for one more, and Ahab names the prophet he hates: Micaiah son of Imlah. Micaiah first echoes the others, then tells what he saw: Israel scattered on the mountains like a flock with no shepherd, and the LORD on his throne asking who will lure Ahab to his death, and a spirit offering to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.

Zedekiah slaps Micaiah; the king sends him to prison on bread and water until he comes back in peace. Micaiah replies that if he does, the LORD has not spoken. In battle Ahab disguises himself, but a random arrow finds the gap in his armor. He dies at evening, propped in his chariot, and the dogs lick his blood at the pool of Samaria. The book closes with short notices of Jehoshaphat of Judah and Ahab's son Ahaziah, who serves Baal like his parents.
readings: Read as a story about true and false prophecy

Four hundred against one: the chapter asks how to know a true prophet. Micaiah's answer is the test of Deuteronomy 18:22, whether the word comes true, and his willingness to say what the king does not want to hear. The court prophets are sincere, perhaps, but they speak with one mouth.
Read as a theological puzzle

How can the God who does not lie send a lying spirit? Readers have answered: God uses or permits deception as judgment; God tells Ahab the truth about the lie, so he is warned; the scene is a parable, not a literal debate; or it reflects an early theology that later writers refined. The note on 22:22 sets out the views.
Read as history

Historians debate whether Ahab died at Ramoth-gilead. Assyrian records show him allied with Damascus in 853 BC, and some think the battle story was first told of a later king. Others think the alliance broke up soon after Qarqar and that Ahab died fighting his former ally in 853 or 852 BC.

views.H: Ahab died in battle at Ramoth-gilead in about 853 BC, as Micaiah and Elijah foretold. 2 Chronicles 18 retells the same events, adding that the LORD helped Jehoshaphat when he cried out.
views.C: Critical scholars see an older prophetic story about the king of Israel (often unnamed) reworked to tie it to Ahab and to Elijah's prophecy (22:38). The formula "Ahab lay down with his fathers" (22:40) and the Assyrian evidence lead some, following J. Maxwell Miller, to doubt that Ahab died this way. The Greek of this chapter, in Codex Vaticanus, has been revised toward the Hebrew (the kaige revision).
views.A: The Kurkh Monolith names "Ahab the Israelite" at Qarqar in 853 BC; the Mesha Stele recalls Omri's house oppressing Moab; the ivories of Samaria illustrate "the ivory house he built" (22:39). Scale armor of the kind that failed Ahab has been found across the region.
views.J: The Talmud says Jehoshaphat distrusted the four hundred because true prophets never use identical words (Bavli Sanhedrin 89a), and identifies the lying spirit as the spirit of Naboth, sent away from God's presence because no liar may stand there (Bavli Sanhedrin 89a; Bavli Shabbat 149b).
views.X: Christian readers see in Micaiah the lonely true prophet, struck on the cheek like Jesus before the high priest (John 18:22); hear in "like a flock with no shepherd" the words Jesus uses of the crowds (Mark 6:34); and read the lying spirit alongside Paul's warning that God sends delusion on those who refuse the truth (2 Thessalonians 2:11).

deep.h: The lying spirit: a careful look
deep.b:
Micaiah's vision raises one of the hardest questions in the Old Testament. The LORD, enthroned among the army of heaven, asks, "Who will lure Ahab?" A spirit volunteers to be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets, and the LORD sends it. Yet Scripture insists that God does not lie (Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2; Hebrews 6:18).

Readers have answered in several ways, and each answer has serious defenders. Judgment by permission: God allows a deceiving being to carry out a sentence on a king who has refused the truth many times (20:42; 21:20); compare Ezekiel 14:9 and 2 Thessalonians 2:11. Calvin took the scene as proof that God governs even evil spirits without being the author of evil. The truth about the lie: R. W. L. Moberly argues that the key is that Micaiah tells Ahab everything; the vision unmasks the deception, and the king who still goes is not deceived without warning. A prophetic parable: some readers, ancient and modern, think Micaiah describes in the language of a royal court what he knows to be true, that the prophets are deceived and the king is doomed, without claiming a literal debate in heaven. Development of thought: critical scholars note that early texts trace harm as well as good to the one God (Isaiah 45:7; 2 Samuel 24:1), while later texts speak of Satan (1 Chronicles 21:1; Job 1), and that ancient Near Eastern texts also speak of gods deceiving as judgment (J. J. M. Roberts). The rabbis identify the spirit as Naboth's, demanding justice, and say God sent it out of his presence because liars may not stand there (Psalm 101:7).

What every reading shares is the end of Micaiah's speech: "The LORD has spoken disaster against you" (22:23). Whatever the spirit did, God's word to Ahab was true, and Ahab chose not to believe it.

The Chronicler, writing perhaps in the fourth century BC, retells this chapter almost word for word because it concerns a king of Judah, Jehoshaphat. The differences show his interests. He opens by saying Jehoshaphat had become Ahab's in-law and that Ahab won him over with a feast (2 Chronicles 18:1–2). He has "God" where Kings has "the Lord" (22:6; 2 Chronicles 18:5). When Jehoshaphat cries out in battle, he adds that the LORD helped him and lured the attackers away (2 Chronicles 18:31). And he follows the story with a prophet's rebuke of Jehoshaphat for helping the wicked (2 Chronicles 19:1–3). He leaves out everything about Ahab's burial and the dogs. Kings tells the story to show the end of Ahab; Chronicles tells it to show the rescue and correction of Jehoshaphat.

echoes: 2 Chronicles 18:1–34; 2 Chronicles 19:1–3; Deuteronomy 18:21–22; Numbers 27:17; Isaiah 6:1–8; Job 1:6–12; Jeremiah 23:16–22; Ezekiel 14:9; Micah 1:2; Mark 6:34; 2 Thessalonians 2:11; 21:19

settings.what: The four hundred prophets say "Go up"
settings.by: the king's prophets, about four hundred, and Zedekiah son of Kenaanah
settings.to: Ahab king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah, sitting on thrones at Samaria's gate
settings.when: when Ahab plans to retake Ramoth-gilead from Aram and Jehoshaphat asks for a word from the LORD
settings.why: All the prophets promise victory with one voice, and Zedekiah acts it out with iron horns. They speak what the king wants to hear. Jehoshaphat's question, whether there is still a prophet of the LORD, shows he does not trust them. The scene raises the question readers faced again and again: how can you tell a true prophet from a false one when they all use the LORD's name? (Compare Jeremiah 28.)

settings.what: Micaiah's first answer and his vision of scattered sheep
settings.to: the king's messenger, then King Ahab
settings.when: after the messenger urges him to agree with the others
settings.why: Micaiah swears he will speak only what the LORD tells him. He first echoes the others, in a tone that makes Ahab demand the truth. Then he tells of Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd, which means the king will die. The picture of the shepherd-king returns in Ezekiel 34 and in Jesus' words in Mark 6:34.

settings.what: Micaiah's vision of the LORD's council
settings.to: King Ahab and King Jehoshaphat, with all the prophets present
settings.when: after Ahab complains that Micaiah never prophesies good about him
settings.why: Micaiah describes the LORD on his throne with the army of heaven, asking who will lure Ahab to his death at Ramoth-gilead. A spirit offers to be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets, and God sends it. The vision tells Ahab plainly that his prophets are deceived and that disaster is decreed. By telling him, Micaiah also gives him one last chance to turn back, which he refuses.
views: J. J. M. Roberts and others take the vision at its word: God can use deception as a judgment on those who have refused the truth (compare Ezekiel 14:9).
R. W. L. Moberly argued that the point lies in Micaiah's telling it: the vision exposes the deception and invites Ahab to repent, so God's purpose is to warn, not only to deceive.
A picture in the language of the time
Others read the heavenly council as a way of saying that Ahab's own wish to hear only good news is what deceives him.

settings.to: Micaiah, and then the king and all the people
settings.when: after the vision
settings.why: Zedekiah slaps Micaiah, and Ahab sends him to prison on bread and water until he returns in peace. Micaiah answers that if Ahab comes back in peace, the LORD has not spoken through him, and calls all the peoples to listen. That last line repeats the opening of Micah 1:2 and is missing from the Greek, so many think a scribe added it. He applies the test of Deuteronomy 18:22: a true prophet's word comes true. Ahab dies at Ramoth-gilead, and dogs lick his blood (22:38), as Elijah said (21:19). The book's lesson for its readers is that the LORD's word always comes true.

traditions.q: God sends a lying spirit into the mouths of Ahab's prophets (1 Kings 22:19–23). Does God cause evil, or only allow it?
views: God rules even evil spirits and wicked acts, and not by bare permission; Calvin cites this very scene (Institutes 1.18.1). Yet God is not the author of sin: the evil belongs to the creatures, and God's purpose in it is just and holy (Westminster Confession 5.4).

God is in no way the cause of moral evil, but he permits it and can bring good out of it (Catechism 311–312). The scene shows God allowing a sentence of judgment to fall on a king who had long refused the truth.

John of Damascus taught that Scripture often speaks of God's permission as his action, so the text says God sent what he allowed (Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 4.19). God wills only good; evil comes from the free choice of creatures.

Wesley held that God permits sin but never decrees it, and he attacked any teaching that makes God the cause of sin (sermon Free Grace). Ahab is judged because he freely refused the plain warning Micaiah gave him.
